source: Cropper & Morel (2021) Learning programs by learning from failures (Popper)
finding: Popper learns from failed hypotheses: too general prunes generalisations, too specific prunes specialisations. These constraints make search far faster than plain enumeration.
numbers: Buttons task (p=20 and p=200 buttons, 10 runs, 1 minute limit): Enumerate solves only n=3 and n=1 required buttons; Popper solves n=10. Evens program: Enumerate 159 s, Popper 4 s.
limits: Toy, robot and list domains. Authors' own system and benchmarks. No noise handling in this version.
agent_relevance: S2/S3 loop should mirror this: a failed candidate should yield a rule that prunes a whole family of candidates, not just itself.

source: Cropper & Morel (2021) Popper vs Metagol, Aleph, ILASP
finding: Popper equals or beats Metagol on all 10 list tasks in accuracy except finddup (Metagol 2 points higher). Aleph struggles on recursive tasks. Popper beats ILASP2i and ILASP3 on grid worlds.
numbers: Accuracy of Popper and Metagol almost identical until about 10,000 examples; then Metagol misses the 1 minute limit and falls to 50% default accuracy. Popper still works at 20,000 examples. Popper time under 1 s for list length 50 and 500.
limits: Accuracy 50% means timeout, not wrong rule. Authors' benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Cheap test of a candidate on all examples scales better than reasoning over the examples inside the search (matches G3: check by code).

source: Cropper & Morel (2021) limit: no noise
finding: Popper needs a hypothesis that entails all positives and no negatives, so it does not support noisy examples in this version.
numbers: No noise experiments in the paper. Authors say noise handling will likely raise learning times.
limits: Fixed in later work (see MaxSynth).
agent_relevance: An exact-fit filter is brittle if any example or check is wrong; keep a best-so-far candidate with partial fit.

source: Cropper & Morel (2021) hypothesis size, Aleph comparison
finding: No single learner dominates. Set-covering learners such as Aleph are fast but tend to give over-specific programs and struggle with recursion.
numbers: On the buttons task Aleph beats Popper on the small dataset when n>8; on the big dataset Popper beats Aleph when n>3.
limits: Mixed result depends on dataset size.
agent_relevance: Keep more than one candidate generator rather than one favourite method.

source: Cropper & Dumancic (2022) Inductive logic programming at 30
finding: Survey. Newer ILP (meta-interpretive learning, ASP-based) learns recursion and invents predicates, generalises from few examples, gives readable rules. Weak spots: noise, scale, predicate invention without user help.
numbers: Qualitative; no pooled effect sizes. States ILP can generalise from small numbers of examples, often one.
limits: Written by ILP developers, not neutral. Claims not retested here.
agent_relevance: Giving the model a rule template (metarule) is how ILP tames the search; S2 prompts can carry templates.

source: Cropper & Dumancic (2022) noise, neural ILP and predicate invention limits
finding: Entailment-based ILP copes with mislabelled labels by covering most positives, but not with observational noise in structured examples. Most neural ILP systems need metarules or templates and fail at predicate invention, recursion and abduction. Predicate invention in general needs user guidance.
numbers: Only Neural Logic Machines avoid metarules; only Abductive MIL joins neural learning with predicate invention, recursion and abduction (survey claim). POPPI cited as exception that invents predicates automatically.
limits: Survey claim, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a neural or LLM rule learner removes the need for structure hints. Constrain what new concepts the model may invent.

source: Evans & Grefenstette (2018) Learning explanatory rules from noisy data (dILP)
finding: Differentiable ILP learns logic programs by gradient descent and tolerates mislabelled examples, unlike classical ILP of that time.
numbers: At 10% mislabelled data it finds a perfect answer in 5 of 6 tasks; sometimes still good at 20-30%. Keeps respectable error when 70% of integer pairs are held out (MNIST pair task, 96% correct cut-off because the digit classifier is 98% accurate).
limits: Hyperparameters were chosen so each task was solved in at least 5% of random initialisations (arbitrary cut-off). One task solved only 30% of seeds.
agent_relevance: Soft scoring of rule candidates tolerates noise; but single runs are unreliable, so sample several and check each.

source: Evans & Grefenstette (2018) dILP limits
finding: Main limit is memory: restricted to nullary, unary and binary predicates and small datasets. An MLP baseline failed the Fizz task because it did not learn the general rule.
numbers: Authors report high memory use; arity at most 2.
limits: Does not scale; later survey also says neural ILP is limited.
agent_relevance: Gradient-style rule search is not a good model for our agent; use propose and test with an executor.

source: Muggleton et al. (2018) Ultra-strong machine learning: comprehensibility of programs learned by ILP
finding: Defines comprehensibility of logic programs as measured human performance after reading them. Two experiment sets; comprehension depends on program complexity and on anonymous invented predicate names.
numbers: From a search snippet only: Metagol chosen for human trials. Exact numbers not read.
limits: Only search summary seen, so treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Name any new concept the model proposes in readable terms.

source: Ai, Muggleton, Hocquette, Gromowski, Schmid (2021) Beneficial and harmful explanatory machine learning
finding: A machine-learned rule helps humans only if it fits a cognitive window (bounded search space and low cost to apply). A rule outside the window can make people worse than unaided.
numbers: Mechanical Turk: 90 participants, 58 mid-performers split 29 self-learning vs 29 machine-aided. Category win_2: machine-aided better after training (p=0.028). Category win_3 (complex theory): performance fell after explanations (p=0.005). win_1: no benefit. Student sample (4 vs 9 people) gave no effect.
limits: Small samples, 5% significance with no correction, student results conflicted, raw data on request only.
agent_relevance: A correct rule is not enough. If a rule is long or costly to apply, a reader (human or model) can do worse with it. Prefer short rules.

source: Hocquette, Niskanen, Jarvisalo, Cropper (2023) Learning MDL logic programs from noisy data (MaxSynth)
finding: Replacing exact fit by a minimum description length trade-off (program size against training fit, solved with MaxSAT) lets learning from failures cope with noise.
numbers: 42 tasks: paired t-test p<0.01, MaxSynth beats Popper on 25/42, ties 13/42, loses 4/42. Works up to about 30% noise; Popper and Aleph struggle from 10%. iggp-rps with noise: Popper and Aleph under 55%, MaxSynth over 90%. Zendo: at least 94%. Noisy constraints cut learning time by 99% (109 s to 2 s in one case).
limits: Authors' own benchmarks. MDL as optimality criterion can fail if the true program is not the shortest.
agent_relevance: Use a complexity-penalised score to choose among candidate rules when checks are noisy; supports a simplicity prior in S3.

source: Hocquette et al. (2023) MaxSynth: statement on the noise criticism
finding: The authors say the common criticism that ILP cannot handle noise is unfounded: most ILP can, but they struggle with noise plus recursion plus predicate invention.
numbers: Cites Cropper and Dumancic 2022. Overhead on noiseless data is small (Table 1 comparison against Popper).
limits: Position statement by authors.
agent_relevance: Distinguish 'cannot handle noise' from 'cannot handle noise and complex programs'.

source: Zhang, Xu, Yilmaz, Liu (2023) A critical review of ILP techniques for explainable AI
finding: Review with a small benchmark comparison: Popper, dILP and dNL-ILP reach 100% on the benchmark tasks; Metagol reaches 100% except the even problem; Aleph struggles.
numbers: Table IX of the review. Notes Metagol is sensitive to example order and wants examples in increasing size.
limits: Small benchmark; solution space large; induced solutions sensitive to noise (authors' abstract).
agent_relevance: Example order can change the learner result; test candidates under shuffled example order.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: hypothesis refinement (main result)
finding: GPT-4 is a good rule proposer when a symbolic interpreter filters its rules. Using the LM as its own interpreter fails.
numbers: Task accuracy: ACRE direct (IO) 28.0, self-refine with LM interpreter (T=3,N=5) 32.0, symbolic-interpreter refinement 45-48. MiniSCAN IO 0.0 vs refinement T=3,N=1 46.0 (raw 77.0). List Functions IO 39.6 vs 42-52. MiniARC: refinement worse than IO (raw 5.9-12.8 vs 33.1).
limits: GPT-4-0613 only. MiniARC is the counterexample. Self-consistency majority vote gave no gain (ACRE 29.0 vs 28.0).
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3: a code-run interpreter filters candidates; model self-judging does not.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) induction-application gap
finding: The model proposes rules it cannot apply. The gap between induction and application is large.
numbers: MiniSCAN task accuracy falls from above 80% (symbolic interpreter) to almost zero when the LM applies its own rules.
limits: Authors say humans and LMs setups differ; gap is an indicator, not proof of mechanism.
agent_relevance: Never let the model execute its own rule; run it in code.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) noise robustness and human comparison
finding: LM refinement degrades even with a single noisy example and falls further with more. Telling it to expect noise helps but does not remove the drop. Humans also fall, but less.
numbers: Noise 12.5%, 25%, 50% of 8 exemplars (List Functions). Inter-annotator Cohen kappa 0.15 for clarity ratings and 0.54 for supportiveness.
limits: Low kappa for clarity means that rating is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Rules built from few examples are fragile; drop or vary examples and see whether the rule survives.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) human reference scores cited
finding: Human reference points: children aged 3-4 solve ACRE blicket in 2 trials; adults about 80% on MiniSCAN (range 65-88%); 45.9% average on List Functions (Rule 2020); about 80% of ARC tasks; 90.9% ConceptARC.
numbers: Numbers quoted by the paper from other studies (Gopnik 2001, Lake 2019, Rule 2020, Johnson 2021, Moskvichev 2023).
limits: Different setups; reference only.
agent_relevance: List Functions is hard for people too (45.9%), so do not expect it to be solved.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Propose natural-language hypotheses, implement them as Python, run on the examples. Beats direct prompting on four datasets.
numbers: ARC (100 random tasks, GPT-4): direct 17%, program only 23%, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected 33%, human-written 45%. 1D-ARC: direct 39.6, program only 61.1, full 73.1. List Functions: 31, 59, 69. SyGuS 94.3% vs DSL baseline CrossBeam 74.8%.
limits: GPT-4 only. Icecuber (DSL solver, no LLM) got 43% on the same ARC sample. Parsel helped with human hypotheses (47.5%) but hurt with LLM hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2/S3: separate the abstract hypothesis from code, test by execution.

source: Wang et al. (2024) hypothesis search: where the bottleneck is
finding: Hypothesis quality is the bottleneck, not code writing. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 ARC tasks. Of 30 tasks solved with summaries, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising.
numbers: Human-selected hypotheses led to correct programs for 33 of 49 tasks (67%). Summarising 64 hypotheses to 8 raised accuracy from 23% to 30%.
limits: Human selection is not an automated step.
agent_relevance: Spend budget on diverse hypotheses and a selector rather than more code samples.

source: Gandarela, Carvalho, Freitas (2025) Inductive learning of logical theories with LLMs
finding: An LLM with feedback from a Prolog engine competes with Popper on noisy theory induction, but long predicate chains are hard.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 average F1 about 0.25 above Popper under noise. GPT-4o F1 about 2x GPT-3.5 at noise 0.1 and 4x at noise 0.3; GPT-4o 21x Llama3-8B at noise 0.1. LLM wall time about 3 orders of magnitude less than Popper.
limits: CHAIN category: no LLM beat Popper at any noise level. Compute very different (GPU vs serial CPU). Synthetic data. Refinement iterations 1 to 4 not monotonic; no gain beyond 3.
agent_relevance: Iterate at most about 3 times with real engine feedback; long chains need explicit decomposition.

source: Gandarela et al. (2025) error analysis by model
finding: Small models fail on syntax; large models fail on logic. Model size does not predict noise resilience.
numbers: Syntactic vs logical errors: GPT-4o 0%/100%, GPT-3.5 0%/100%, Llama3-8B 46%/54%, Mixtral-8x7B 20%/80%, Gemma-7B 100%/0% (no valid Prolog). Mixtral F1 dropped over 0.8 from noise 0.1 to 0.2.
limits: Narrow model set, 2024-era models.
agent_relevance: Run a syntax check first; logic errors need counterexamples from the engine.

source: Helff et al. (2026) SLR: automated synthesis for scalable logical reasoning (SLR-Bench)
finding: 19k ILP-style single-rule induction prompts in 20 curriculum levels, scored by a Prolog judge. LLMs write valid rules but often wrong ones; the bottleneck is semantic, not syntax.
numbers: Accuracy basic/easy/medium/hard: o3 99/93/74/45 (cost $207 for the run); gpt-5 100/90/72/46 ($103); gpt-4o 93/29/20/ about 0; base models solve under half of easy. GPT-4o to o3 doubles accuracy with +1777% tokens and +1034% cost. CoT adds about 5%.
limits: Single clean rule, perfect judge. Table columns partly garbled in text extraction, so read gpt-4o hard figure with care. Authors' benchmark.
agent_relevance: Scale and test-time compute help but hit a wall on multi-clause rules; plan decomposition.

source: Helff et al. (2026) SLR: training and diminishing returns
finding: Curriculum fine-tuning with verifiable rewards doubles Llama-3-8B accuracy and reaches parity with Gemini-Flash-Thinking at lower cost. More compute can hurt on a tier.
numbers: Ordered curriculum beat random and reverse. o4-mini-high vs o4-mini: overall LRL 12.8 vs 12.3 but medium tier 40% vs 52%. Transfer gain +17 on MMLU high school statistics.
limits: Training claims, not scaffold claims. Transfer gains reported by authors only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more thinking always helps; keep checks per tier.

source: Li et al. (2024) LLMs for relational reasoning: how far are we?
finding: Compared GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 7B/13B with a Differentiable Logic Machine (DLM) on logic-program induction tasks. The small neural-symbolic model wins.
numbers: DLM (60k parameters, trained on 10 samples) reaches 100% F1 on several tasks at both sizes. GPT-4 gets 100% on HasFather but 49.05% on IsUncle. GPU memory 429 MiB for DLM vs 36,957 MiB for LLM.
limits: Chain-of-thought did not consistently help. 2023-era models; synthetic family and graph relations.
agent_relevance: LLMs degrade as the target rule has more predicates and on larger instances; test candidates on larger held-out cases.

source: Peng et al. (2025) ILP-CoT: abductive rule induction with MLLMs and ILP
finding: Qwen-7B proposes rule structure; this is turned into Metagol metarules and Metagol induces the rule. Beats direct prediction and custom CoT by a large margin.
numbers: CLEVR-Hans accuracy val/test: direct 54.76/51.60; custom CoT 34.44/35.85; ILP-CoT 88.37/81.85; NEUMANN (specialised) 96.67/97.43. Swap backend: Popper 25.53/46.74; ILASP out of time at the 5 minute cap; Metagol finishes in about 10 s.
limits: One benchmark per ablation, authors' system. Structure proposals stay correct even when perception hallucinates.
agent_relevance: LLM proposes the shape (template), solver fills it: matches S2 propose and S3 check.
